claims.text: Lightweight HEAs can uniquely combine low density, high mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance through the synergy of lattice-distortion strengthening and protective oxide formation.
Al, Ti, and Cr are suitable low-density substitutes for heavier alloying elements.
Replacing heavy elements with Al, Ti, and Cr lowers the overall alloy density.
The proposed low-density element substitutions introduce significant atomic-size mismatch and enhanced lattice strain.
Substitution-induced lattice distortion increases strength by impeding dislocation motion.
An Al- and Cr-containing alloy can form a dense Al2O3/Cr2O3 surface oxide during exposure to air at 900 °C.
Chromium promotes formation of a dense Al2O3/Cr2O3 layer in FeNiCuAlCr.
The engineered lightweight HEA will form fine, stable Al2O3/Cr2O3 oxide precipitates on its surface.
A continuous, adherent Al2O3/Cr2O3 film slows high-temperature oxidation kinetics by acting as a barrier.
The protective oxide film reduces aqueous chloride corrosion by acting as a chemical barrier.
Relative to the baseline, the engineered alloy will have lower density.
Relative to the baseline, the engineered alloy will maintain or increase yield strength.
Relative to the baseline, the engineered alloy will have a lower corrosion current density in 3.5 wt.% NaCl.
Relative to the baseline, the engineered alloy will have a lower parabolic oxidation rate constant at 900 °C because of its Al2O3/Cr2O3 layer.
Conventional HEAs commonly have densities that impede weight-sensitive applications.
A conventional HEA lacking the proposed substitutions or oxide-forming balance typically has poorer corrosion and oxidation behavior.
Extreme chloride concentrations or sufficiently high temperatures can destabilize or spall the protective oxide and eliminate its corrosion and oxidation benefits.
Processing variations can produce insufficient lattice distortion to maintain mechanical strength, thereby breaking the proposed property synergy.
